q: Across a period from left to right, the first ionisation energy of the elements generally:
o: First decreases and then stays constant
x: Nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell, so the outer electrons are held more tightly and are harder to remove.

q: Down a group, electronegativity decreases mainly because:
o: Atomic size increases, so the nucleus attracts bonding electrons less strongly
Nuclear charge decreases down the group
The number of valence electrons decreases
x: New shells are added, the bonding pair is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so attraction for it falls despite the larger nuclear charge.

q: Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine, yet its electron affinity is less negative. The reason is that:
o: The small, crowded 2p subshell of F repels an incoming electron strongly
Fluorine has a smaller nuclear charge than chlorine
Fluorine already has a complete octet
The incoming electron enters the 3d subshell of fluorine
x: In the very small fluorine atom, electron–electron repulsion in the compact 2p subshell partly cancels the attraction for an added electron.

q: The Na⁺ ion is much smaller than the Na atom because:
o: The nucleus gains protons when the ion forms
Removing the 3s electron removes the whole outer shell
The ion has more electrons than the atom
Shielding increases when the electron is lost
x: Na is 2,8,1 and Na⁺ is 2,8; losing the third shell, with the same 11 protons pulling on fewer electrons, makes the ion much smaller.

q: Removing one electron from a gaseous N atom needs more energy than removing one from a gaseous O atom. Why?
o: Nitrogen has a larger nuclear charge than oxygen
Oxygen's outer electron is in a higher shell
Nitrogen has a stable half-filled 2p subshell, while oxygen's paired 2p electron is repelled and easier to remove
Nitrogen atoms are larger than oxygen atoms
x: N is 2p³ (half-filled, each orbital singly occupied). In O (2p⁴) one orbital holds a pair, and repulsion makes one of those electrons easier to remove.

q: The bond energies of the hydrogen halides fall in the order H–F > H–Cl > H–Br > H–I. This is because, from HF to HI:
o: The bond length increases as the halogen atom gets larger
The bond length decreases as the halogen atom gets smaller
The number of bonds between the atoms decreases
x: Larger halogen atoms give longer bonds with poorer orbital overlap, so the bond becomes weaker; HI is the easiest to break.

q: The reduction of nuclear attraction on valence electrons caused by the inner electrons is called the shielding effect. Down a group, shielding:
o: Increases, which helps lower the ionisation energy
Decreases, which raises the ionisation energy
Stays constant, so ionisation energy is unchanged
x: More inner shells are present further down a group, so shielding increases and the outer electron is removed more easily.

q: The first four ionisation energies of element X are 738, 1451, 7733 and 10540 kJ mol⁻¹. X is most likely in:
x: The big jump comes after the second electron, so X has two outer electrons and the third comes from an inner shell; X is a Group II element (magnesium).

q: The d-block elements are also known as:
x: The d-block lies between the s- and p-blocks and its elements are called transition elements.

q: The element with atomic number 15 is placed in:
x: Z = 15 is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p³ (phosphorus): the last electron enters 3p, n = 3 gives period 3, and five outer electrons give Group VA.

q: How many groups (vertical columns) make up the p-block of the periodic table?
x: A p subshell holds 6 electrons, so the p-block is 6 columns wide. The s-block has 2, the d-block 10 and the f-block 14.

q: The lanthanides and actinides together make up the:
x: In the lanthanides and actinides the differentiating electron enters 4f or 5f orbitals, so they form the f-block.

q: Helium is placed with the noble gases in Group VIIIA (18), although its electronic configuration, 1s², is actually that of:
x: Helium's last electron enters an s orbital, so by configuration it is s-block; it is placed with the noble gases because of its filled shell and inertness.

q: The block to which an element belongs is decided by:
o: The number of neutrons in its nucleus
The number of shells in its atom
The subshell that receives the last (differentiating) electron
x: s-, p-, d- and f-blocks are named after the subshell being filled by the last electron. The number of shells gives the period, not the block.

q: Where in the periodic table is an atom with outer electrons 3d⁵ 4s² (argon core) placed?
x: The last electrons fill 3d, so it is d-block; the outermost shell is n = 4 (period 4); 5 + 2 = 7 outer electrons put it in Group VIIB (manganese).

q: Sodium and potassium are stored under kerosene (paraffin oil) because they:
o: React quickly with air and water
x: Alkali metals react rapidly with oxygen and moisture, so they are kept under an unreactive oil.

q: A few drops of phenolphthalein are added to water after sodium has reacted with it. The solution turns pink because it contains:
x: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂; the NaOH formed makes the solution alkaline, turning phenolphthalein pink.

q: A small piece of sodium dropped into water floats and melts into a silvery ball. This shows that sodium has:
o: A high density and a high melting point
A low density and a low melting point, and the reaction is exothermic
A low density, and the reaction absorbs heat
A high melting point, and the reaction is slow
x: Sodium is less dense than water, so it floats; the heat released by the reaction is enough to melt it because its melting point is low (about 98 °C).

q: The anion present in sodium peroxide is:
x: Peroxides contain the O₂²⁻ ion with oxygen at −1. O²⁻ is the oxide ion and O₂⁻ is the superoxide ion.

q: 4.6 g of sodium reacts completely with water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. What mass of sodium hydroxide is formed? (Na 23, O 16, H 1)
x: Moles of Na = 4.6/23 = 0.2; the ratio Na : NaOH is 1 : 1, so 0.2 × 40 = 8.0 g NaOH. Halving the moles gives the wrong 4.0 g.

q: Potassium superoxide, KO₂, is used in breathing equipment in submarines and spacecraft because it:
o: Absorbs oxygen and releases carbon dioxide
Absorbs water vapour and releases hydrogen
Absorbs carbon dioxide and releases oxygen
x: 4KO₂ + 2CO₂ → 2K₂CO₃ + 3O₂: exhaled CO₂ is removed and fresh oxygen is supplied.

q: The hydroxides formed when alkali metals react with water become stronger bases down the group. Which is the strongest base?
x: Down Group I the M–OH bond becomes more ionic as the cation gets larger, so CsOH releases OH⁻ most readily and is the strongest base.

q: Sodium peroxide reacts with carbon dioxide: 2Na₂O₂ + 2CO₂ → 2Na₂CO₃ + O₂. In this reaction the oxygen of the peroxide ion is:
x: Peroxide oxygen is −1. Some becomes −2 (in Na₂CO₃, reduced) and some becomes 0 (in O₂, oxidised), so it disproportionates.

q: When an alkaline earth metal M burns in chlorine gas, the salt produced has the formula:
x: Group II metals form M²⁺ ions, so two Cl⁻ ions are needed for each metal ion: M + Cl₂ → MCl₂.

q: When Group II metals react with water they form hydroxides, M(OH)₂. Down the group, the solubility of these hydroxides in water:
o: Decreases, so Ba(OH)₂ is the least soluble
Increases, so Mg(OH)₂ is the most soluble
Increases, so Ba(OH)₂ is the most soluble
x: Mg(OH)₂ is almost insoluble, Ca(OH)₂ is slightly soluble and Ba(OH)₂ is fairly soluble, so solutions become more strongly alkaline down the group.

q: Calcium reacts steadily with cold water, while magnesium reacts only very slowly with it. This is mainly because calcium:
o: Has a smaller atom and higher ionisation energies
Forms a more insoluble hydroxide that protects it
Has a larger atom and lower ionisation energies, so it loses its outer electrons more easily
Has more valence electrons than magnesium
x: Reactivity of Group II metals increases down the group as atoms get larger and the two outer electrons are lost more easily.

q: Magnesium reacts with cold water at first, but the reaction soon almost stops. The main reason is that:
o: Magnesium becomes coated with magnesium chloride
A layer of sparingly soluble Mg(OH)₂ forms on the surface
Hydrogen gas dissolves in the water
x: Mg + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂; the hydroxide is almost insoluble and coats the metal, slowing further attack. Hot water or steam reacts faster.

q: Which Group II chloride has the most ionic character?
x: Ba²⁺ is the largest Group II ion with the lowest polarising power, so BaCl₂ is the most ionic; BeCl₂ is largely covalent.

q: 2.4 g of magnesium burns completely in oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. What volume of oxygen at STP is used? (Mg = 24; 1 mol gas = 22.4 dm³)
x: Moles of Mg = 2.4/24 = 0.1; O₂ needed = 0.1/2 = 0.05 mol; 0.05 × 22.4 = 1.12 dm³. Forgetting the 2 : 1 ratio gives 2.24 dm³.

q: Magnesium burnt in air forms some magnesium nitride, Mg₃N₂. When water is added to the ash, a gas with a sharp smell is given off. The products are:
x: Mg₃N₂ + 6H₂O → 3Mg(OH)₂ + 2NH₃; the pungent gas is ammonia, with nitrogen still at −3.

q: Which of these Group IV elements is a typical metal?
x: Metallic character increases down Group IV: carbon is a non-metal, silicon and germanium are metalloids, and tin and lead are metals.

q: Silicon dioxide dissolves in hot concentrated sodium hydroxide to form sodium silicate, Na₂SiO₃. This shows that SiO₂ is:
o: An amphoteric oxide that reacts only with acids
x: SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O: reacting with a base to form a salt and water is the behaviour of an acidic oxide.

q: On going down Group IV from carbon to lead, the stability of the +4 oxidation state:
o: Decreases, while that of the +2 state increases
Increases, while that of the +2 state decreases
Stays the same for all elements
Decreases, and so does that of the +2 state
x: Because of the inert pair effect, the ns² pair is held more firmly in heavier elements, so +2 becomes more stable than +4 towards lead.

q: Tin(II) chloride, SnCl₂, is commonly used as a reducing agent because:
o: Sn(+2) is readily oxidised to the stable Sn(+4) state
Sn(+2) is readily reduced to tin metal
Chloride ions in it are strong oxidising agents
Sn(+4) is less stable than Sn(+2)
x: For tin, the +4 state is still the more stable one, so Sn²⁺ easily loses two electrons and reduces other species.

q: Which oxide of carbon is a neutral oxide?
x: CO neither forms an acid with water nor reacts with bases under normal conditions. CO₂ and SiO₂ are acidic, and PbO is amphoteric.

q: The thermal stability of the Group IV hydrides MH₄ changes down the group. Which is the least stable?
x: As the atom gets larger the M–H bond becomes longer and weaker, so stability falls from CH₄ to PbH₄, which hardly exists.

q: Silicon reacts with warm sodium hydroxide solution: Si + 2NaOH + H₂O → Na₂SiO₃ + 2H₂. Which statement is correct?
o: Silicon is oxidised from 0 to +4 and hydrogen is released
Oxygen is given off and silicon is unchanged
It is a neutralisation with no change in oxidation number
x: Si goes from 0 to +4 in Na₂SiO₃, and hydrogen from +1 to 0 in H₂, so this is a redox reaction typical of a non-metal with alkali.
